name: OCD Test
tagline: Check how much obsessive thoughts and compulsions affect your days.
intro: This screener looks at five areas linked to obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD): fear of contamination, checking and doubt, unwanted thoughts, order and symmetry, and mental rituals or reassurance seeking. Answer based on how often each statement has applied to you over the past month. It takes about five minutes. It is not a diagnosis, but it can help you understand your patterns and decide whether to seek support.
seoTitle: OCD Test: Free obsessive compulsive screener
seoDescription: Do unwanted thoughts, checking or washing take up your time? Take this 5-minute OCD screener and get a personal report on five areas.

contamination.name: Contamination and washing
contamination.short: How much fear of dirt, germs or contamination drives what you do.
contamination.low: Your answers suggest that fear of dirt or germs plays only a small role in your life. You care about hygiene in a normal way and can let it go once you have washed. That flexibility is healthy: you protect yourself without letting cleanliness take over your time. Keep it that way by noticing if washing or cleaning starts to grow during stressful periods, as that is often when such habits creep in.
contamination.mid: Your answers suggest that worries about dirt or germs regularly influence what you touch, wash or avoid. You may clean or wash a bit more than others, or feel uneasy in certain places. This can still be manageable, but it is worth keeping an eye on. Try gently delaying a wash by a few minutes and notice that the discomfort fades on its own. If the habits keep growing, talk to your doctor.
contamination.high: Your answers suggest that fear of contamination takes up a lot of your time and energy, for example through long washing, cleaning or avoiding places and people. This can be exhausting and can make daily life smaller. These patterns are common in OCD and respond well to help, especially a form of cognitive behavioural therapy called exposure and response prevention. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional about what you notice.

checking.name: Checking and doubt
checking.short: How often doubt makes you check, recheck or seek certainty.
checking.low: Your answers suggest that you usually trust what you have done and rarely feel the need to check things again. A quick check now and then is normal, especially when you are tired or in a hurry, and it does not seem to hold you back. This trust in your own memory saves time and stress. Keep relying on it, and notice if doubt starts to grow during busy or uncertain times.
checking.mid: Your answers suggest that doubt sometimes makes you check doors, appliances, messages or your work more than needed. This can cost time and leave you feeling uneasy even after checking. A helpful step is to check once, with full attention, and then say out loud what you saw. Try to resist the second check and notice that the uneasy feeling fades. If checking keeps increasing, talk to your doctor.
checking.high: Your answers suggest that doubt and checking take up a lot of your day and can make you late or leave you drained. Checking often brings only short relief before the doubt returns, which keeps the cycle going. These patterns are common in OCD and can be treated well, for example with cognitive behavioural therapy that focuses on exposure and response prevention. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional.

intrusive_thoughts.name: Unwanted thoughts
intrusive_thoughts.short: How much unwanted, upsetting thoughts or images bother you and how seriously you take them.
intrusive_thoughts.low: Your answers suggest that unwanted thoughts rarely upset you. Almost everyone has strange or unpleasant thoughts now and then, and you seem able to let them pass without attaching much meaning to them. That is a real strength. Keep reminding yourself that a thought is just a thought and says nothing about who you are or what you will do.
intrusive_thoughts.mid: Your answers suggest that unwanted thoughts or images sometimes upset you and are hard to shake off. You may worry about what they mean or try hard to push them away, which often makes them come back more. It can help to notice the thought, label it as just a thought and let it be there without arguing with it. If these thoughts start to take up a lot of your time, talk to your doctor.
intrusive_thoughts.high: Your answers suggest that unwanted, upsetting thoughts are a big part of your days and that you take them very seriously. This can be frightening and lonely. It helps to know that such intrusive thoughts are a well known feature of OCD and do not mean you want them or will act on them. They respond well to treatment, such as cognitive behavioural therapy. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional.

order.name: Order and symmetry
order.short: How strongly you need things to be orderly, even or feel just right.
order.low: Your answers suggest that order and symmetry are not a big concern for you. You may like things tidy, but you can live with some mess or change without feeling tense. That flexibility makes daily life easier for you and the people around you. If you ever notice that arranging or redoing things starts to take more time, treat it as a sign that your stress level may be rising.
order.mid: Your answers suggest that you often feel a need for things to be in order, even or done in a certain way. A preference for order is fine, but if it brings tension when things are different, it can start to cost energy. Try leaving one small thing slightly out of place and notice how the uneasy feeling fades over time. If the need for things to feel right keeps growing, talk to your doctor.
order.high: Your answers suggest that a strong need for order, symmetry or a just right feeling takes up a lot of your time and causes tension when things are different. This goes further than simply liking tidiness. These patterns are common in OCD and respond well to help, such as cognitive behavioural therapy. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional, who can help you loosen these rules step by step.

rituals.name: Rituals and reassurance
rituals.short: How often you use counting, repeating, mental reviewing or reassurance to calm anxiety.
rituals.low: Your answers suggest that you rarely need rituals or reassurance to feel calm. You seem able to sit with some uncertainty and let uneasy feelings pass on their own. That is a valuable skill, because rituals tend to bring short relief but make anxiety stronger in the long run. Keep trusting that discomfort fades without you having to fix it.
rituals.mid: Your answers suggest that you sometimes use counting, repeating, mental reviewing or asking for reassurance to calm yourself. This brings relief, but it can also teach your brain that the worry was dangerous. Try to delay a ritual or a reassurance question by a few minutes and notice what happens to the feeling. Telling a trusted person what you are working on can help. If rituals keep growing, talk to your doctor.
rituals.high: Your answers suggest that rituals, mental reviewing or seeking reassurance take up a large part of your day and are hard to stop. You may know they make little sense and still feel you must do them. That is a typical sign of OCD, and it is not a personal failing. Effective treatment exists, especially cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention. Please talk to your doctor or a qualified mental health professional.

summary: This screener shows how strongly you recognise five groups of obsessive and compulsive patterns. Higher scores mean these patterns showed up more often in the past month. Many people have odd thoughts or small habits now and then; OCD is about how much time, distress and disruption they cause. The results are not a diagnosis. Only a qualified professional can assess this, and OCD responds well to treatment.
